title: 5X2
full_review:
5X2" (ThinkFilm) is an austere but finely acted and perceptive story of the unraveling of a contemporary marriage told in five sequences in reverse order.

Directed by Francois Ozon, best known on these shores for "Swimming Pool," the film could almost be mistaken for an Ingmar Bergman work, in its clinical, unsparing look at a disintegrating union. The backward-moving device has been used before, most notably in Harold Pinter's play (and later film) "Betrayal," and it is quite intriguing, in this instance, to trace the relationship to its roots.

The film begins with the couple dividing up their assets, and deciding on such matters as the custody of their child, in front of a divorce lawyer. When their separation is official, surprisingly, the couple go to a hotel room, and go through the ritual of one last bedroom encounter.

Marion (Valeria Bruni-Tedeschi) seems to crave tenderness at that moment, but then changes her mind. The aroused Gilles (Stephane Freiss) bluntly forces himself on her regardless. (Be warned: there's full nudity in this scene.) You wonder how that relationship could have ended with such a brutal act. After Marion showers, they have one final talk during which Gilles suggests getting back together, but a solemn Marion has no interest, and leaves.

The next sequence (the first of four flashbacks) takes place just after their child is born. They're having company: Gilles' gay brother and his younger lover. The two men have an open partnership, and the brother tolerates his companion's occasional infidelities. Gilles admits he and Marion once went to a party that turned into an orgy, and he freely participated with men and women.

Then we flashback to Marion's difficult childbirth. She had a blocked placenta, and labor had to be medically induced. She calls Gilles at his office, but though he says he'll be right over he can't bring himself to come to the hospital. When he finally does, his mother-in-law chastises him for not being at his wife's bedside, but he seems not to be able to bear watching Marion go through the painful process. Other episodes include their wedding ceremony and the eventful evening that followed, and their romantic meeting, which is not what was expected.

Ozon's measuredly paced "scenes from a marriage" is quite fascinating, as it reveals layer by layer the over-the-years affection, betrayals, foibles and idiosyncracies, making the final parting ultimately clear.

Marion and Gilles are played impeccably by Bruni-Tedeschi and Freiss. Their actions are not always honorable, but the characters are presented in all their flawed humanity. The sexual content, particularly the scene described above, is raw, but the style is more scientific than exploitative.

The film is in French with English subtitles.

The film contains a graphic sex scene with female frontal nudity, a gay subplot, frank sexual talk, premarital and postmarital sexual situations, discussion of artificial insemination, and rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
